wcs_p1_a: Weeks in and nothing much is changing? I'd want to quit too, or else keep doing the exact same thing forever so I never had to find out. Before either one, I'd look for what exactly is in the way. Sometimes those weeks were mostly reading about it and getting ready to, which can feel a lot like doing it (this article included). Or you did sit down with your little one, and fear got there first, or a part of you that's trying to protect you. It can be as plain as never having the place to yourself. Whatever it turns out to be, I'd work on that one thing instead of giving up on everything.
wcs_p2_a: Say you've been trying to comfort your little one, but the loving grown-up isn't really there yet. Your little one would notice, the way you notice a hug from someone who's checking their phone. More loving words won't fix that, and I wouldn't decide reparenting is useless over it, either. I'd borrow that grown-up first. Then try again, and see if your little one can tell the difference.
wcs_p2_b: Say you've been trying to comfort your little one, but the loving grown-up isn't really there yet. Your little one would notice, the way you notice a hug from someone who's checking their phone. I'd probably want to fix it by saying sweeter and sweeter things, which won't work, and I wouldn't decide reparenting is useless over it, either. I'd borrow that grown-up first. Then try again, and see if your little one can tell the difference.
wcs_p3_a: And if something does shift, I'd be careful how much I decide it means. Ten minutes of relief, and then it's back, is ten minutes of relief. I'd still take it, but it doesn't mean the problem's over, or even that the exercise did it, since a good night's sleep can do that too. If it helps, make one note of what changed and how long it lasted. Checking on it every day would only turn into more checking.
wcs_p3_b: And if something does shift, it's tempting to think, that's it, it worked. Ten minutes of relief, and then it's back, is ten minutes of relief, though. I'd still take it! It just doesn't mean the problem's over, or even that the exercise did it, since a good night's sleep can do that too. If it helps, make one note of what changed and how long it lasted, and leave it there. Checking on it every day would only turn into more checking.
wcs_p4: How many tries is enough? I really don't know, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who promises you a number, including you, since some things shift in a day and some take about as long as learning guitar. If it's making things worse, or you just can't do it right now, I'd stop or change course sooner. Not wanting to do it anymore can be a reason too, but if that "nope" sounds like a part of you that's trying to protect you, I'd hear it out first. And if you keep following the reparenting steps correctly without getting the expected results, consider if you have a unique case these steps don't match yet. Maybe you'll find something that works better for you, or you can ask me what I'd do for this case, or ask a therapist you work with. Either way, I'd like to hear about it!
wcs_p5_a: And sometimes the exercise itself goes really well. You feel real care for your little one, you say exactly what needed saying, and then the rest of the week looks just like before. I wouldn't go looking for a deeper meditation yet, or decide this one failed. Maybe it just hasn't made it out of the exercise. Whatever the grown-up did in there, maybe comforting or slowing things down, I'd try about five percent of it out here. That could be telling a friend you're having a rough day instead of saying you're fine, or taking a real break before you're wiped out.
wcs_p5_b: And sometimes the exercise itself goes really well. You feel real care for your little one, you say exactly what needed saying, and then the rest of the week looks just like before. That one's confusing, since it really did seem to work. I wouldn't go looking for a deeper meditation yet, or decide this one failed. Out here, the old way you learned to treat yourself is probably still running things, mostly out of habit, and the grown-up hasn't made it out of the exercise yet. So whatever they did in there, maybe comforting or slowing things down, I'd try about five percent of it out here. That could be telling a friend you're having a rough day instead of saying you're fine, or taking a real break before you're wiped out.
wcs_p6: One small thing you actually follow through on can teach your little one more than ten more good meditations. Afterward, the only question is whether that care got a little more real out here, and what to keep for next time. It isn't a grade on you. You don't need to do this after every session, either, and one small act like that is a start, not proof you've got it all down.
